bib.title: CORAL: An LLM-Native Harness for Production Recommender Systems

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "CORAL: An LLM-Native Harness for Production Recommender Systems", Muhammad Rafay Azhar et al. (Meta AI), preprint arXiv:2609.02730v1 [cs.CL], dated September 2026 (submitted 2 Sep 2026; cover date 3 Sep). No venue.
COVERAGE: all 14 pages, 47,403 chars, read in full: text, Table 1-3, Fig 1-2, limitations, appendix A (sample prompt). References skimmed only. Figures not rendered; captions come from the extracted text. Nothing was skipped. No embedded instructions seen.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- A closed loop around a live recommender improved over successive rounds without retraining. The agent adapts in context from attributed outcomes.
  number: none
  setup: 3 rounds on a video service, each judged by an A/B test. R1 was zero-shot and R3 aggregates several cycles.
  quote: "Recording these attributed outcomes lets the agent reinforce the changes that helped and reverse those that did not, so its decisions improve over successive cycles. This improvement requires no retraining"
  where: p.6, section 4.3
- Retrieval-budget deployment results: sessions +0.16% and watch time +0.15% at no extra serving cost.
  number: +0.16% sessions, +0.15% watch time
  setup: video recommender, converged global allocation, A/B test over millions of users. Budget was consolidated, not expanded.
  quote: "showed a 0.16% increase in video-viewing sessions across all users, alongside a 0.15% increase in total watch time—all at no additional serving cost"
  where: p.7, section 5.1; Table 1 p.6 also shows largest market sessions +0.77%
- Progress was not monotonic. R2 overcorrected and was neutral, and the agent used that outcome to refine.
  number: R1 watch time +0.13%; R2 neutral; R3 watch time +0.15%
  setup: same as above, R1 to R3
  quote: "This progression is not monotonic—the second round did not improve on the first—yet it is precisely the behavior the loop is designed to produce"
  where: p.7, section 5.1
- Per-segment allocation raised sessions for new low-signal users.
  number: +0.23%
  setup: same service, segments by engagement level and tenure
  quote: "This raised video-viewing sessions for new low-signal users by 0.23%."
  where: p.7
- Serving-capacity deployment: round 2 widened the round-1 change to more segments, and savings grew 44% with engagement unchanged.
  number: 44%
  setup: different service, discrete treatment per user segment, A/B test over millions of users, 2 rounds. The absolute savings are not given beyond "millions of USD" annualized.
  quote: "increasing the savings of the first round by 44% while leaving engagement statistically unchanged"
  where: pp.7-8, section 5.2
- The harness fixes the control flow and uses a constrained optimizer so every change fits the budget by construction. The model does not control the flow.
  number: none
  setup: tools are analysis, retrieval, attribution, constrained optimizer (projection onto {s: c_t(s) <= B}) and apply. They run in fixed order each cycle.
  quote: "invoking them in the same fixed order every cycle rather than leaving control flow to the model"
  where: p.5
- Defaults were not tuned: cadence k=3 days, memory m=3 cycles.
  number: k=3, m=3
  setup: both deployments. The authors say they are "sensible defaults rather than tuning them".
  quote: "we set the cadence tok = 3days ... and the memory horizon tom = 3cycles"
  where: p.6
- LLM cost scales with cycles, not users. The total is about 10^6 tokens, or tens of USD per deployment.
  number: ~10 calls/cycle, ~1,500 in and ~2,500 out tokens (retrieval); ~8 calls, ~2,000 in, ~2,500 out (serving)
  setup: Table 2. Token counts are estimated from prompt and payload sizes because the pipelines do not log token usage.
  quote: "the total is on the order of106 tokens ... on the order of tens of U.S. dollars"
  where: p.8, section 6; Table 2 p.7
- The authors say tuning time fell from engineer-weeks to a few days. This is an assertion with no measurement.
  number: "order-of-magnitude"
  quote: "compressing a tuning cycle from several engineer-weeks to a few autonomous days, an order-of-magnitude faster turnaround with no engineer in the loop."
  where: p.8, section 5.3
- Formulation: cumulative shortfall against a moving per-cycle oracle optimum s*_t, subject to budget B (Eq. 1-2). The policy is s_t = pi(o_t, M_t). The memory has three stores: observations, the model's own assessments, and decisions with attributed outcomes.
  where: pp.3-5

LIMITS
- The authors concede three limits (p.9). The loop still runs under human supervision. Only one decision class was tested, constrained resource allocation. Evidence comes from costly, setting-specific A/B tests, and no standard pre-deployment evaluation exists.
- The gains are small, mostly under 1%. There are no confidence intervals, no baseline such as a human-tuned or non-LLM optimizer, and no ablation of memory or attribution. Only 2 and 3 rounds are reported.
- Despite the "no engineer in the loop" wording, a human supervises throughout. The text says guardrails will progressively replace that supervision, but it does not show this has happened.
- Learning in context is inferred from the R1 to R3 trajectory alone. There is no control showing that memory caused the gain.

BUILDS ON: Agentic recommender and self-iteration work: AgentX (Lao et al., 2026), Hu et al. 2026, Liu et al. 2026, Shen et al. 2026. Memory work: Mem0 (Chhikara et al., 2025), MemGPT (Packer et al., 2023), Generative Agents (Park et al., 2023). Tool use: ReTool (Feng et al., 2025). Recommender models: Naumov et al. 2019, Kang and McAuley 2018, Zhai et al. 2024.

CODE: Appendix A, Fig 2 (p.13), a per-cycle decision prompt. Its output schema, verbatim: {"decisions":[{"unit":"<id>","adjustment":"<action from feasible set>","rationale":"<why>","confidence":"high|medium|low"}],"assessment":"<cross-unit synthesis of what is working and what is not>"}. The prompt also says "Select only from this set; do not invent actions." Table 3 (p.14) shows that the two case studies fill the same template with different placeholders.

FIGURES
- Fig 1 (p.4): the CORAL harness. (a) is the control plane: memory, LLM reasoning, constrained optimizer, guardrails, tools. (b) is the loop of observe, reason and recall, optimize and deploy, measure, update memory, on a k-day cycle with the last m cycles as context. It is the quickest picture of a closed self-improving loop with a deterministic budget gate.
- Table 1 (p.6): the R1 to R3 non-monotonic results.
- Fig 2 (p.13): the decision prompt template.

TRIAGE: This is on-topic for loop engineering, as a production example of a self-improving loop with a measured-outcome feedback signal. The best fit is note 08 (self-improving loops). Its claim of in-context improvement from A/B results written back to memory is the core of note 08, so it would only sharpen that note: add a one-line citation plus a references row. Because 08 is over length, put no new prose there. Secondary fits:
- Note 03 (scorekeeper): the A/B experiment plus pre/post attribution acts as the scorekeeper, and the harness writes the result back to memory.
- Note 09 (failure modes): the R2 overcorrection that came out neutral. This is a weak example.
- Note 02 (loop shapes): the fixed-order, fixed-cadence loop with a deterministic projection gate. This is a good small example if a one-line citation is wanted.
Not for note 05 (long-running): the run is cycles of days, with no context-continuity theme.
Weakness for the course: the effect sizes are small and unbaselined, and the human remains in the loop.

PROBLEMS: None. The extraction is clean. Table 1 and the equations came through readable but flattened.
